ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is the transformer primary-side circuit; the primary coil is connected to the AC generator symbol, and ammeter A is connected in series in the primary-side circuit, so A measures the primary-side current. On the right side of the figure is the secondary-side circuit; a resistor R is connected across the two ends of the secondary side, and voltmeter V is connected between the upper and lower ends of the secondary side, in parallel with the load terminal voltage, so V measures the secondary-side terminal voltage, that is, the voltage across load R. Reasoning: The problem statement says that the transformer and meters are all ideal, and that the internal resistance of the generator coil can be neglected. The induced electromotive force of the generator is proportional to the magnetic induction intensity B; when B is reduced to half of the original, the AC voltage output by the generator to the primary side is also reduced to half of the original. The turns ratio of an ideal transformer is fixed, so the secondary-side voltage changes according to the same proportion, and the reading of voltmeter V becomes half of the original. The load resistance R remains unchanged; when the secondary-side voltage is halved, the secondary-side current is also halved. In an ideal transformer, the ratio of the primary-side and secondary-side currents is determined by the fixed turns ratio, so when the secondary-side current is halved, the primary-side current is also halved. Ammeter A measures the primary-side current, so the reading of A also becomes half of the original.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that A measures the primary current and V measures the secondary terminal voltage across the load. From the text, the transformer and meters are ideal and the generator internal resistance is negligible. Since the generator induced emf is proportional to magnetic induction strength B, halving B halves the primary applied AC voltage. With a fixed ideal transformer turns ratio, the secondary voltage is halved, so the voltmeter reading is halved. The resistor R is unchanged, so the secondary current is also halved; by the fixed current ratio of an ideal transformer, the primary current measured by A is halved. Therefore both readings become one-half of their original values.

method.method_draft: From the image, replace the secondary resistor R through the ideal transformer by its reflected impedance on the primary side; the voltmeter does not affect this because it is ideal. The reflected impedance is fixed because R and the turns ratio do not change. From the text, the generator has negligible internal resistance, so the primary circuit is simply the generator emf driving this fixed equivalent impedance through the ammeter. Halving B halves the generator emf, so the primary current through the fixed input impedance, and hence the ammeter reading, halves. The primary terminal voltage also halves, and the ideal transformer ratio is constant, so the secondary voltage across R measured by V halves. Thus both meter readings are reduced to half.
method.CoT_raw:
Image description: The figure shows an ideal transformer. On the left primary side, a generator/AC source is connected in series with an ammeter and the primary coil. On the right secondary side, the secondary coil is connected to a resistor R, and an ideal voltmeter is connected in parallel across the secondary/load terminals.

Reasoning: Since the voltmeter is ideal, it has infinite resistance and does not change the secondary load. The only effective secondary load is the fixed resistor R. Through the ideal transformer, this resistor is reflected to the primary side as a fixed equivalent impedance because neither R nor the turns ratio changes. The generator has negligible internal resistance, so the primary circuit is equivalent to the generator emf driving this fixed input impedance through the ammeter. The generator emf is proportional to the magnetic induction strength B, so reducing B to half reduces the generated emf to half. With a fixed equivalent impedance, the primary current is also reduced to half, so the ammeter reading becomes half. The primary terminal voltage also becomes half, and the transformer turns ratio is constant, so the secondary voltage across R is reduced to half. Therefore the ideal voltmeter reading also becomes half.
